extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Bergson; philosophers and creative writers interested in theories of knowledge, order, and creative activity
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative principles about order, originality, and the nature of artistic/intellectual creation from Bergson's Creative Evolution; useful for thinking about how creative works manifest vitality versus mechanical order. Emphasizes distinctions between geometric/mechanical regularity and the spontaneous, unforeseeable 'vital' order associated with genuine creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order as agreement between subject and object
rubrics_metrics.description: Reality is 'ordered' exactly to the degree in which it satisfies our thought; order is therefore a certain agreement between subject and object — 'the mind finding itself again in things.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an evaluative touchstone: a work shows 'order' when it enables the perceiver to recognize themselves in the object (coherence between intention and perception). The surrounding discussion stresses that order may take different directions (vital vs. geometric) yet still be 'order' by this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish two kinds of order: geometric (second kind)
rubrics_metrics.description: The second kind of order may be defined as geometry (its extreme limit); it is concerned whenever a relation of necessary determination is found between causes and effects and evokes inertia, passivity, automatism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a criterion for creative work, identify features that make the work predictable, determined, mechanically reproducible or governed by necessity. This 'geometrical' order supports generalization and repeatability but tends toward passivity and foreseeability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish two kinds of order: vital/willed (first kind)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first kind of order is that of the 'vital' or of the 'willed', connected with spontaneity, creative progress, and in its highest forms exceeding mere finality; works of art and life in its entirety tend in this direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate creative works for signs of spontaneity, originality, unforeseeability, and a sense of 'continuous creation' — qualities Bergson associates with genuine vitality rather than mechanical repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as an undivided act / poetry as continuous movement
rubrics_metrics.description: When a poet reads verses, one can 'enter into his thought... live over again the simple state he has broken into phrases and words.' Poetry is an 'undivided act' and a continuous movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer works that preserve an indivisible, continuous feeling or creative impulse rather than those that fragment emotion into merely material elements; the unity of the creative act is a mark of artistic vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of materializing feeling by relaxation of attention
rubrics_metrics.description: If attention relaxes, sounds become distinct, words break into syllables, letters 'dance' — increasing extension and mathematical order but representing 'nothing positive' and expressing 'a deficiency of will.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a production guideline, be wary of over-analysing or over-formalizing a living creative impulse; excessive decomposition into technical elements can strip vitality and convert expressive force into mere order or ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical form is artificial and conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: There is something artificial in the mathematical form of a physical law; standards of measurement are conventional and 'foreign to the intentions of nature' — measuring is a wholly human operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or crafting creative work, recognize that strict formal metrics and quantitative measures may misrepresent or miss the genuinely creative aspects; do not conflate technical perfection with vital value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality/generation: different origins of likeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The likeness among living individuals (genera) has a different origin from likeness produced by the same composition of causes; in life the effect can be constant despite differing elementary causes, whereas in the physical case the same causes give the same effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether recurring forms in a genre arise from an underlying living principle (authentic reproduction, variation) or from mechanical repetition; genuine creative likeness implies an indivisible source rather than mere causal repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of deduction in psychological and moral domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduction is feeble in psychological and moral sciences; from a proposition verified by facts, verifiable consequences can be drawn only up to a certain point — one must appeal to 'common sense' and continuous experience to bend deductions along the sinuosity of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating narratives about human life or moral situations, avoid overreliance on purely logical deduction or schematic causality; value nuance, lived experience, and unpredictability that resist strict deductive closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction's dependence on spatial/mathematical imagining
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction rests on the belief causes and effects repeat; it implicitly superposes situations in imagination (placing stove on stove), treating qualities as if they could be superposed like magnitudes — a transparency toward geometrical necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when treating qualitative, temporal, or singular experiences as repeatable regularities; creative works should not be judged solely by their conformity to repeated patterns that belong to the geometrical ideal limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hypostasizing 'disorder' as an absolute absence
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of 'disorder' often denotes the absence of a certain order but to the profit of another; treating disorder as the absence of all order is a pseudo-idea leading to pseudo-problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting surprising, chaotic, or unconventional creative choices, consider whether they express a different order rather than mere absence of order; criticism should seek the operative ordering principle rather than assume nullity.
